                    ### Question
                    A 24-year-old previously healthy man comes to his physician because of dyspnea and hemoptysis for the past week. Examination shows inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. His hemoglobin concentration is 14.2 g/dL, leukocyte count is 10,300/mm3, and platelet count is 205,000/mm3. Urine dipstick shows 2+ proteins. Urinalysis shows 80 RBC/hpf and 1–2 WBC/hpf. An x-ray of the chest shows pulmonary infiltrates. Further evaluation is most likely to show increased serum titers of which of the following?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Immunoglobulin A
opb. Anti-GBM antibody
opc. Anti-dsDNA antibody
opd. Anti-PLA2R antibody
ope. P-ANCA

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of dyspnea, hemoptysis, pulmonary infiltrates, and renal involvement with proteinuria and hematuria suggests a pulmonary-renal syndrome. The most likely diagnosis in this context is Goodpasture's syndrome, characterized by the presence of anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies. This aligns with the reasoning chain that considers Goodpasture's syndrome and the retrieved evidence paths that associate lung infiltration and glomerulonephritis with anti-GBM disease. Other options, such as ANCA-associated vasculitis (P-ANCA) and systemic lupus erythematosus (anti-dsDNA), are less likely given the specific combination of symptoms and the typical age of presentation. Therefore, further evaluation is most likely to show increased serum titers of anti-GBM antibodies.
